issues.item: Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, funerals/cemeteries are not impossible triggers, but they are weakly anchored unless there was a death in the accident or major bereavement content. Nothing else in the profile suggests grief- or death-related cueing, so this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for a life-threatening accident. The other items center on fear, disorganization of memory, hypervigilance, and damaged self-view, but do not indicate betrayal by authorities, emergency response, or organizational negligence. This appraisal therefore appears insufficiently supported by the trauma context and accompanying items.

vignette: Talia was driving home along the coastal highway when the delivery truck ahead hydroplaned. There was no screech, only the sickening crunch of shearing metal and the violent deployment of the airbag against her sternum. When she awoke, the moment had fractured into disjointed shards. She could not tell a clear story of what happened even to herself, and the memories refused to put themselves in the right order. Because the trauma-related events refused to cohere, the fragmented recall instantly brought back the full memory of the impact without warning. This unmoored recall convinced her that she had permanently changed for the worse, that she could not trust that she would do the right thing, and that the world was a dangerous place. In turn, these negative appraisals distorted how she processed the event, causing her to focus exclusively on catastrophic details that fractured her recall further. Her conviction that the world remained dangerous quickly rewired her physiological state; her nervous system locked into a state of high alert, manifesting as a startle response that made her feel jumpy or easily startled. The constant physiological readiness meant she felt unsafe unless her back was against a wall where she could see the room, a posture she had to maintain even in her own consulting office. The fear that she had permanently changed for the worse also dictated her daily habits; she tried hard to control her emotions in every interaction, masking her tremors with professional detachment. This rigid emotional control, combined with a deep aversion to vulnerability, led her to avoid sex, leaving her divorced home increasingly silent. She also began avoiding sleep, terrified that going to sleep or lying in the dark would allow the unmoored memories to surface unchecked. The cycle tightened rapidly. Her heightened threat state disrupted her cognitive processing, meaning her nightly waking alert actively prevented her from consolidating a coherent narrative, which meant the confused sequence of memories only deepened. This fragmented recall then fed back into her appraisals, reinforcing her self-doubt and belief that she was permanently damaged, which in turn kept her on high alert. To manage the escalating physiological arousal, she clung tighter to her maladaptive strategies, trying hard to control her emotions and strictly avoiding sleep. Yet these avoidance behaviours only guaranteed that her nervous system remained trapped in threat mode; by suppressing her distress and avoiding intimacy, she denied her brain the natural decay of emotional intensity, ensuring that her startle response and need to keep her back to the wall persisted unbroken. Worse, her inability to sequence the event meant that everyday triggers were misinterpreted as active threats. Her heightened threat state made ordinary trauma-related events impossible to ignore, and the sound of tires braking or even a close call in her own driveway instantly flooded her with unwanted thoughts and vivid crash imagery, which in turn convinced her the world remained a dangerous place. As months passed, the strain manifested most acutely at work. Sitting at her heavy oak desk to conduct psychopharmacology consultations became unbearable; she could not look at her own charts without her mind jumping to the twisted dashboard of her sedan. She began refusing evening hospital calls, citing phantom chest pains that were actually the somatic echo of her crash imagery. What finally brought her to seek help was a hypervigilant panic attack during a telehealth session with a former resident, where she accidentally left her camera on and he saw her frantically shuffling her papers to align with the corner of the room. She knows that without intervention she will remain trapped in this loop, forever doubting her clinical judgment and unable to walk through a parking lot without bracing for impact. She hopes to reclaim her life and her profession, but she is most afraid that she is irreparably broken, that the accident took her capacity for safety and left her with nothing but a permanently damaged nervous system.
